newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say they push back army assault.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say they push back army assault.

text.p: Zaire's army has launched a counter-offensive against rebels trying to topple the government of military strongman Mobutu Sese Seko from a swath of territory in the east, the rebel leader said on Monday.
Laurent Kabila told journalists in the eastern town of Goma that government forces attacked positions in and around Fizi at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Sunday night but were beaten back by Monday morning.

Kabila, who heads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), said his forces had captured many weapons and dead bodies abandoned by the fleeing army but there was no independent confirmation.
"The Zaire army left a lot of weapons and dead bodies in the field when it retreated," Kabila said. He did not give precise casualty figures.
Kabila said a smaller attack had also taken place at Itombwe, 40 km (25 miles) from Uvira, and that the army again was pushed back.
The alliance that began the rebellion three months ago with a group of mostly ethnic Tutsis, now occupies a 500 km (300 mile) swath of eastern Zaire along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
Mobutu, Zaire's president for over 31 years, last week named a new government whose primary responsibility is to crush the rebels.
The sprawling central African country with vast mineral resources is facing its worst crisis in decades and so far Zaire's ragged and poorly paid army has been unable to turn back the rebel advance.
Kabila said Mobutu's army had attacked from the city of Lubumbashi and Kalemie in the copper and cobalt-rich mining region of Shaba and that his soldiers would pursue them.
"We will drive them back to wherever their bases are," he said.

Since the ragged and poorly paid army was routed from the eastern Zaire in October a popular army commander with combat experience, General Mahele Bokoungo, has been appointed with new powers to organise the demoralised troops for battle.
Last week the rebels said they had driven back another counter offensive in the north of their occupied strip and captured the town of Bunia in a gold-mining region.

Although people from the region have confirmed that Bunia was taken the government says there is still fighting around the town and little news has filtered down the 360 km (220 mile) road to the largest rebel stronghold at Goma.
Bunia is on the threshold of vast gold and mineral resources in the Upper Zaire province, and was one of the few remaining airstrips in the east used by the army to bring reinforcements.
It is also at the head of one of the few passable roads in the region west to Kisangani, the biggest city in the east, in the heart of the jungle and which the rebels have threatened to target.

Kabila said that Burundian Hutu rebels of the Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD), which is fighting to overthrow Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army junta, had set ambushes for vehicles on the road from Bukavu to Goma although he did not give any figures for casualties.
The Burundian rebels were driven from bases in eastern Zaire and their headquarters at Uvira by the ADFL, which is closely allied to Tutsi armies in both Burundi and Rwanda.

Uvira, once a strategic base for Burundian Hutu rebels waging war against Bujumbura's Tutsi army junta, was the second town to be captured by the rebels after they took nearby Kamanyola on the Rwandan border three months ago.
Africa's latest conflict was sparked off by Zairean attempts to expel back to Rwanda the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group that migrated to Zaire up to 200 years ago.
The Banyamulenge, backed by Rwanda's battle-hardened Tutsi-dominated army, resisted and took up arms to fight for their rights as Zaireans.
